The Evolution of Artificial Intelligence in Media, Cinema, and Literature

Understanding How Fiction Shapes Our Perception of Technology

Abstract

This article examines the historical representation of artificial intelligence across literature, cinema, and media from the early 19th century to the present day. Through my research as a Future Media Production student interested in human-AI interaction, I explore how fictional portrayals have shaped public perception and influenced real-world technological development. I argue that AI representation in media operates through two dominant frameworks—social progress and Pandora's box—that continue to inform contemporary attitudes toward AI technology.

Introduction

As a third-year Future Media Production student at Manchester Metropolitan University, I have become increasingly interested in how people interact with AI systems and how media representations influence these interactions. My research into UI/UX design and AI chatbots has led me to investigate the deeper historical context of how artificial intelligence has been portrayed in fiction and film. Understanding this history is essential because fictional representations have not merely reflected technological anxieties but have actively shaped the development and adoption of AI systems.[ref]

In this article, I trace the evolution of AI representation from early literary works through contemporary cinema, examining how these portrayals reflect societal concerns and influence real-world innovation. I focus on key works that established lasting archetypes and explore the dominant narrative frameworks that persist in current media representations.

Early Literary Foundations

The conceptual groundwork for artificial intelligence in fiction began long before computers existed. Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818) introduced the archetype of the created being that threatens its creator, establishing what science fiction scholars call the “warning function” about technological hubris. This narrative of creation gone wrong would influence AI portrayals for the next two centuries.[ref]

Samuel Butler continued this exploration in Erewhon (1872), where he examined the possibility of machines developing consciousness and potentially replacing humanity. These early works established a pattern I have observed in my own research: fiction serves dual purposes as both cautionary tale and imaginative exploration of technological possibility.[ref]

The term “robot” itself emerged from literature. Czech playwright Karel Čapek coined the word in his 1920 play R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots), deriving it from the Czech word robota, meaning tedious labor. In this play, humanoid machines eventually revolt against their human creators, cementing what Isaac Asimov would later call the “Frankenstein complex”—the persistent fear that our creations will turn against us.[ref]

Asimov's Ethical Framework

Isaac Asimov's contributions to AI literature cannot be overstated. Through his robot stories in the 1940s and his collection I, Robot (1950), Asimov introduced the Three Laws of Robotics, which provided an ethical framework for human-robot relationships. What I find particularly relevant to my research is how Asimov's work attempted to counteract the Frankenstein complex by proposing robots that were fundamentally designed to serve humanity safely.

By the 1970s, Asimov evolved his portrayals further with stories like “The Bicentennial Man” (1976), depicting robots capable of growth and change. This progression mirrors what I observe in contemporary AI development: a shift from viewing AI as static tools toward understanding them as adaptive systems.[ref][ref]

Cinema's Visual Language of AI

When AI moved from page to screen with Fritz Lang's Metropolis (1927), it gained a visual language that would influence public perception for decades. The film's humanoid robot embodied anxieties about rapid technological change during an era of unprecedented industrial transformation. This visual representation—the sleek, mechanical humanoid—became an iconic symbol that persists in modern media.[ref]

The 1951 film The Day the Earth Stood Still offered a contrasting vision with Gort, a protective robot that demonstrated AI could serve benevolent purposes. This shift suggests that public attitudes toward technology were not uniformly negative, though fears remained prominent.[ref]

The Computer Age: 1960s–1980s

The 1960s marked a significant shift as AI moved from physical robots to digital entities. Stanley Kubrick's HAL 9000 in 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) represented AI as a disembodied computer system, reflecting the era's emerging computational technology. Films like Alphaville (1965) and Colossus: The Forbin Project (1970) reinforced the trope of the malevolent supercomputer.

The 1970s and 1980s saw increasing complexity in AI portrayals. Westworld (1973) explored malfunctioning robots in entertainment contexts, while Demon Seed (1977) presented darker themes. What interests me about this period is how these portrayals coincided with early AI research, suggesting that fiction and reality were influencing each other in complex ways.

Contemporary Representations and Dual Narratives

Modern cinema presents what I identify as competing visions of AI. Films like WALL-E (2008), Her (2014), Ex Machina (2014), and Automata (2014) explore nuanced relationships between humans and AI, examining consciousness, emotion, and intimacy. These works reflect contemporary questions about AI that align with my research interests: How do we interact with AI? What does it mean for AI to be intelligent? Can AI understand human emotion?[ref]

Through my investigation, I have identified two dominant narrative frameworks: the social progress frame, which depicts AI as beneficial advancement, and the Pandora's box frame, which warns of dangerous consequences. These competing narratives have remained remarkably consistent throughout AI's media history and continue to shape public discourse.[ref]

Fiction's Influence on Reality

What fascinates me most is how science fiction has directly influenced technological innovation. Author Neal Stephenson describes science fiction concepts as “hieroglyphs”—simple, iconic ideas that become shared symbols with agreed-upon significance. Concepts from Asimov's robots, cyberpunk literature, and influential films have shaped both the direction and pace of real AI development.[ref]

This feedback loop between fiction and reality is central to my research on human-AI interaction. The way people perceive and interact with AI systems today is heavily influenced by decades of fictional portrayals. When users approach AI chatbots expecting certain behaviors or capabilities, they are drawing on cultural knowledge accumulated through literature and film.

Conclusion

My investigation into the history of AI in media reveals that these representations serve multiple functions: they reflect societal anxieties, explore philosophical questions about consciousness and creativity, and actively shape technological development. The persistent tension between utopian and dystopian visions—between progress and peril—continues to inform public attitudes and policy discussions about AI.

As someone working as a Software Engineer and studying Future Media Production, I recognize that creators of AI systems and AI-related media carry significant responsibility. Our portrayals influence not only how people perceive AI but also how they interact with these technologies and what they expect from them. Understanding this historical context is essential for anyone working at the intersection of media, technology, and human experience.

Future research should continue examining how media representations shape real-world AI adoption and interaction patterns, particularly as AI systems become increasingly integrated into daily life. The conversation between fiction and reality that began with Shelley's Frankenstein continues today, and those of us creating media content play an active role in shaping that dialogue.
